Since the Garde Arts Center opened in 1926, it has been a gathering place where generations of the New London community have experienced the arts.

Yesterday, I presented the Garde with a Congressional Record statement from my office recognizing its 100th anniversary and its enduring contributions to New London and southeastern Connecticut.

Even through uncertain times, the Garde Arts Center has remained at the center of cultural and educational life in Connecticut and will remain that way for generations to come. I was glad to make the Garde’s century of history part of the permanent Congressional Record.

Happy National Public Lands Day! Oregon’s public lands are places to hike, fish, explore and more.

I joined my colleagues in supporting a resolution recognizing 618 million acres of public lands across the country and the many ways they support our communities. I’ll keep fighting to protect these lands for generations to come.

Bring this up at trivia night: Roughly 34% of LA County is protected public land, which helps ensure we’re never too far away from the great outdoors. The challenge that falls on us now is to safeguard these lands.

I introduced legislation like the Rim of the Valley Corridor Preservation Act with Sen. Adam Schiff to ensure these public lands remain accessible and protected for generations to come.

I am deeply concerned by the seizure of airports in Tigray and the suspension of flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire. The people of northern Ethiopia have already lived through a devastating war, and roughly one million remain displaced from it. They cannot afford another one.

The 2022 peace agreement was hard won, and every party has a responsibility to honor it. I urge the Tigray People's Liberation Front and the federal government to step back from confrontation, protect civilians, and return to dialogue with the support of the African Union. The United States should use its diplomatic weight to keep this peace from collapsing

Since its establishment in 1999, the Office of the Special Envoy for Holocaust Issues (SEHI) has been the only office in the federal government solely devoted to pursuing justice for Holocaust survivors and advocating on their behalf. For decades, SEHI has worked with foreign governments, international institutions, and Jewish organizations to pursue restitution and compensation for survivors and their families, recover Nazi-looted property, preserve Holocaust memory, and address unresolved Holocaust-era obligations.

As the number of living Holocaust survivors continues to decline, this work is only becoming more urgent, amplifying the need to appoint a career official as the next SEHI, with the seniority, diplomatic experience, and specialized expertise necessary to negotiate complex restitution and compensation matters. I was proud to work with @RepNadler and members of the Congressional Jewish Caucus to urge Secretary Rubio to preserve the Special Envoy for Holocaust Issues position as a distinct and permanent office. This work is too important to be consolidated or eliminated, and we will continue to fight for the pursuit of justice on behalf of Holocaust survivors and their families.

ICYMI: Earlier this month, I was honored to join military and community leaders in Chicopee for the ribbon-cutting ceremony for Westover Air Reserve Base’s new Regional ISO Maintenance Hangar.

After years of steadfast advocacy from local, state, federal, and military leaders, this long-awaited project is now complete, marking a significant investment not only in Westover's infrastructure, but also in the men and women who carry out the base's mission every day.

This Hispanic Heritage Month, I’m thinking about their story and the countless Latino families whose hard work, sacrifice, and determination have helped build this country. I’m also thinking about whether that same dream is still within reach for families today.

At a time when immigrants are too often treated as threats instead of neighbors, and families who came here searching for a better life are living in fear, we cannot lose sight of what has always made this country extraordinary.

My family’s story is uniquely American. Now more than ever, we need to fight to keep that promise alive for the next generation.

No, Mr. President, Americans want Congress and you to do your job protecting humanity, protecting our utility bills, and protecting us from out-of-control, corrupt greed.

A principal role for government is to protect the American people. Safety must always be our first mandate. It is also the government’s job to protect the American people from unmitigated greed. The billionaires that you are listening to now would prefer the government stay on the sidelines. But the U.S. government knows how to regulate corporate greed and how to address new technologies that could destroy our world.

The robber barons of the Gilded Age amassed enormous fortunes while working families struggled. Soon thereafter, unchecked Wall Street speculation and a devastating stock market crash helped plunge America into the Great Depression.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Democrats responded with landmark reforms to rein in Wall Street, protect working families, and prevent another financial catastrophe. They established the Securities and Exchange Commission to police the stock market, created Social Security to provide economic security for Americans, and enacted the first federal minimum wage to protect workers from exploitation.

When we invented and exploded the atomic bomb in New Mexico in 1944, the scientist who oversaw it, J. Robert Oppenheimer, said, “now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.” He realized that this new technology could mean the end of humankind. After Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the United States, Congress, and our top scientists worked to limit the spread of nuclear weapons, even while many of the scientific inventions coming out of that discovery made their way into our business community and way of life.

What we do now will matter. We cannot just let AI and data centers regulate themselves or depend on their goodwill to lower utility costs and limit the most destructive possibilities inherent in this rapidly evolving technology. We must let local communities have a say in what is built in their neighborhoods so they can protect their water, environment, and cost burdens. 

But Congress must act. There must be a strong, enforceable national regulatory framework. We must have civil and criminal liability. We must protect the local and national financial interests of working families.

It is not a hoax, Mr. President. And we have a job to do.

Emmett Till was robbed of his life but also of his own unique Black future. And to remember him is to honor not only the life stolen from him, but the one he deserved to live.

This weekend, I visited "If Emmett Till Lived," the powerful new exhibition in Chicago that affirms the fullness of the man he could have become.

I was honored to select a work of art and contribute a reflection for this exhibit, and it was a joy to spend time with the visionary @sarahelizalewis and Rev. Wheeler Parker Jr., Emmett's cousin, best friend, and last surviving witness to his kidnapping, who helped bring it to life.

For the first time, I invoked Emmett Till's name and didn't feel heaviness. Instead, I was immersed in blissful opportunities to imagine him as a father, a husband, and a Black man who loved softball and dreamed of being a police officer.

While the strange fruit of Black bodies hang from trees across America and Black history is under attack, exhibitions like these are a necessary reminder not only of America's legacy of lynching and racial terror—but also of the Black futures that are lost when Black lives are stolen.

It's why I'll continue demanding a thorough, transparent, and comprehensive federal investigation into the suspicious deaths of Black folks found hanging across the country, as authorized by the Emmett Till Antilynching Act of 2022.
